The source spectrum has evenly spaced harmonic lines. In this example they are **100 Hz apart**. Passing through the tract changes each harmonic’s **amplitude**, its height in the spectrum, according to how close it lies to a formant.
children: Harmonics near a formant are stronger; harmonics far from the formants are weaker. The filter shapes existing source frequencies instead of creating an extra harmonic at each formant.

teaching.text: For **schwa**, the formant targets are approximately **500, 1,500, 2,500 and 3,500 Hz** in this example. The filtered spectrum has groups of tall harmonic lines near those targets and lower lines between them.

**The harmonic frequencies stay in the same places while their heights change.** The source controls the spacing between the narrow lines; the tract’s formants control the broad pattern of tall and short lines.
children: The **spectral envelope** is the outline across the harmonic heights. Its broad peaks reveal the vowel’s formant pattern, while the individual narrow peaks remain harmonics of the source.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The **/i/ filter** has a low first formant and a high second formant. The example marks **F1 at 300 Hz and F2 at 2,300 Hz**. These are the air resonances favored by this vowel shape, not the source’s fundamental frequency.

The **same source supplies harmonic lines every 100 Hz**. The /i/ tract makes the lines near F1 and F2 strong and leaves many lines between them weak. That produces a low cluster of tall peaks, a wide quieter region and another cluster near the higher F2.

**The filter changes harmonic amplitudes, not their frequency locations.** A line at 100, 200 or 300 Hz remains at that frequency; its height can change. Moving the formants changes which of the existing source harmonics receive the strongest response.
The higher marked resonances, **F3 and F4**, are the third and fourth formants. Together with F1 and F2 they shape the broad **spectral envelope**, the outline across the harmonic heights.
children: The vowel is identified by this pattern of resonances and strengths. The large gap between F1 and F2 is the central /i/ feature in this comparison.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: The **/a/ filter** brings the first two formants closer together. The example marks **F1 at 750 Hz and F2 at 1,200 Hz**, giving a higher F1 and lower F2 than the /i/ example.

The source still provides **harmonics every 100 Hz**. The tract favors the existing harmonics near its formant targets, so strong lines gather into a lower, more closely grouped region instead of the widely separated F1 and F2 groups of /i/.

**The same harmonic frequencies can carry different vowels.** Changing the filter changes the heights of the lines, while the lines remain at the source frequencies. A formant between two harmonics can strengthen neighboring harmonics without adding a new source line at the formant frequency.
children: For example, the 750 Hz formant lies between source harmonics at 700 and 800 Hz. Those neighboring source frequencies can be strengthened without creating a new harmonic at 750 Hz.

teaching.text: The broad **spectral envelope** follows the strengths of those lines. Its peaks reflect F1, F2 and the higher formants, while the narrow individual peaks reflect the harmonics. This separates the vowel’s tract resonances from the vibration rate of the voice.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** describes one short instant of sound. Its horizontal axis is frequency and its vertical axis is amplitude. Speech changes as the tongue and lips move, so a single spectrum cannot show the whole change.

A **spectrogram** places successive spectra along time. **Time runs horizontally, frequency runs vertically and darkness represents amplitude.** A dark area contains stronger energy at that frequency and moment; a pale area contains less.
children: Tall spectral peaks become dark marks at their frequency positions. Repeating this through time makes the stronger resonant regions appear as bands.

teaching.text: During **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the two formant bands are far apart. As the sound changes into **/a/**, the low band rises and the higher band falls: **F1 rises and F2 falls**.
children: The moving dark bands track changing formants. Their changing positions come from changing vocal-tract shape, while the spectrogram preserves when those changes occur.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **“Where were you a year ago?” is connected speech that changes over time.** Producing the phrase involves moving between sounds, so the tongue and lips keep changing the air passage rather than holding one vowel shape throughout.
A **spectrogram** can show those changing resonances across the phrase. Time locates each part of the utterance, frequency locates the formant bands and darkness indicates the strength of the sound.
children: A spectral slice describes one moment. Following the bands across time is what reveals how the vocal-tract resonances develop through connected speech.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: **Formants are revealed by how they shape the source harmonics.** When harmonics are closely spaced, many lines fall around each resonance, so their changing heights trace the formant envelope clearly.
The example begins with harmonics at **100, 200, 300 and 400 Hz**, with F1 near **300 Hz** and F2 near **2,100 Hz**. Many harmonic lines are available around both resonances.
children: Increasing the harmonic spacing to **250 Hz** leaves fewer lines in the same frequency range. A formant can fall between those lines, making its location less obvious in the measured spectrum.

teaching.text: **Raising F0 spaces harmonics farther apart; it does not by itself move the formants.** Holding the vowel filter fixed can therefore give a smooth-looking spectrum at low F0 and a sparse, ambiguous-looking spectrum at high F0.

A toddler’s harmonics can be spaced by about **400 Hz**, while a soprano’s can be spaced by about **800 Hz**. Those wider intervals make the formant pattern harder to recover from the available harmonic peaks.
children: The difficulty is identifying the tract’s broad resonances from a smaller set of source frequencies. A tall isolated harmonic is not automatically the exact location of a formant.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** form one of the two major vibrating systems involved in voiced speech. They are a membrane held around its edges. Different regions can move together or against one another while the outside edges remain constrained.

A **membrane mode** is a coordinated movement pattern across that surface. **(1, 1)** has one broad moving region. **(2, 1)** and **(1, 2)** divide the motion into two opposing regions along different directions.
children: The **(2, 2)** pattern has four alternating regions, and **(3, 1)** has three regions along one direction. These numbers describe the spatial divisions of one surface, not separate membranes.

teaching.text: The combined surface adds all five mode movements at each point. Where their contributions agree, the displacement is larger; where they oppose one another, the contributions partly cancel. The result changes shape even though each component has a regular pattern.

The spectrum at the pickup has five component peaks. The displayed **100 to 500 Hz** are assigned harmonic frequencies for this illustration, and the equal peak heights are arranged at the pickup. They are not a calculation of the natural frequencies of every rectangular membrane.

For the voiced source, the lowest harmonic is called **F0**, and the other harmonics occur at multiples of that fundamental. Different voices can have different F0 values while retaining that regular spacing. **F0 describes the source**, while F1 and F2 describe resonances of the air above the vocal folds.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A string with **one fixed end and one free end** must remain still at the fixed bottom while allowing maximum oscillatory motion at the top. The bottom is a **node** and the top is an **antinode**.
The first mode goes from that still bottom to the moving top in one **quarter-wave**. The next allowed modes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves into the same length.
children: Those counts give frequencies at **one, three, five and seven times the fundamental**. For the displayed 100 Hz fundamental, the four frequencies are 100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz.

teaching.text: An even quarter-wave count would end with a node at the top, which conflicts with the freely moving end. **The endpoints decide which patterns are possible.** The second allowed mode is therefore the third harmonic multiple.
When all four modes contribute, their spectrum has peaks at those four frequencies. The equal peak heights reflect the chosen contributions at the free-end measurement point.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency relative to a fixed–fixed string. Matching the lowest frequency across the two demonstrations requires separate tuning.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** connects a point of no movement with a point of largest movement. Mode 1 contains one packet from the fixed bottom to the free top.
The numbered stacks show **three packets for mode 2, five for mode 3 and seven for mode 4**. Adding one packet would reverse the condition at the top; adding two preserves the required antinode.
children: The packets occupy progressively shorter parts of the same string. More packets mean a shorter spatial pattern and a faster repetition rate.

teaching.text: The allowed frequencies therefore follow **1 : 3 : 5 : 7**. The counts name quarter-wave sections of each whole-system pattern. They do not mean that the second mode has a second, separate string or that its frequency must be twice mode 1.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is the second vibrating system. The passage can be treated as a tube extending from the vocal folds through the mouth to the lips. Its walls are formed by the surrounding tongue, palate and throat.
The idealized tube is **closed at the glottis and open at the lips**. Air displacement is constrained at the closed end, while air can oscillate back and forth at the open end.
children: This is longitudinal motion: the air moves along the passage. Compression occurs when neighboring portions move closer together, and expansion occurs when they separate.

teaching.text: In the mass–spring model, **mass represents air’s inertia** and **stiffness represents its restoring response to compression**. The masses and springs describe two properties of the air, rather than objects inserted into the tract.
**Mode 1 gives F1**, the lowest air resonance, and **mode 2 gives F2**, the next one. In the uniform fixed–free reference, mode 2 is three times as fast as mode 1.
children: The markers locate **/a/ near one-third**, **/i/ near two-thirds** and **/u/ at the lips**, measured from the glottis. What each mode does at the marked place determines the effect of narrowing it.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: **Air displacement and air compression describe different changes.** Displacement is back-and-forth movement from a resting position. Compression is a reduction in the spacing between neighboring air elements, alternating with expansion.

Where neighboring elements move together while keeping about the same spacing, the air acts mainly as a **moving mass**. Where the elements repeatedly bunch together and spread apart, the air acts strongly through its **springiness**.
children: Near a displacement node, one location can remain almost still while air on either side moves toward and away from it. That region can have strong compression despite little displacement.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, the closed glottal end has constrained motion and strong compression nearby. The freely moving lip end has large displacement with little compression. In higher modes, more regions of displacement and compression alternate along the same tract.

**A constriction must be evaluated within the particular mode.** Added effective mass has a large effect where air moves strongly. Added stiffness has a large effect where compression changes strongly. A fixed location can therefore have different effects on F1, F2 and F3.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: The marked locations identify different parts of an **air-mode pattern**. A region dominated by springiness has strong repeated compression and expansion; a region dominated by moving mass has strong back-and-forth displacement with relatively little change in spacing.

At **A**, the air is strongly springy. **B** is dominated by moving mass. At **C**, neighboring air regions bunch together and expand while the marked location moves very little, so C is also strongly springy.
children: A motionless location does not imply that the air around it is inactive. Neighboring elements can change their spacing strongly there.

teaching.text: For the **third mode**, constricting at **C** increases both effective mass and stiffness. The extra mass has little effect because local displacement is small. The extra stiffness strengthens a region that is already compressing and expanding strongly, so **F3 rises**.

The prediction follows from the local movement, rather than from the letter attached to the location. At a different place in the same mode, or the same place in a different mode, the relative importance of mass and stiffness can change.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: A **constriction** narrows the air passage. The MRI views locate that narrowing within the actual tongue, lips and throat. **High/low** describes tongue height and **front/back** describes how far forward the tongue lies.
**Dean** has a high front vowel, with a constriction near **two-thirds of the distance from the glottis**. **Don** has a low back vowel, with a constriction near **one-third of that distance**.
children: The glottis is the opening between the vocal folds. These fractions locate the constriction along the tract; they are not frequency ratios.

teaching.text: **Dune** has a high back vowel with **lip rounding**, so its important free-end loading occurs at the lips. **Done**, containing schwa, is the neutral, relatively uniform reference. **Dan** has a low front vowel.

The vowel shape determines **where effective mass and stiffness increase**. The same kind of narrowing can lower one resonance and raise another because the air’s motion and compression differ between modes at that place.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: **Constriction increases both effective mass and stiffness.** Narrowing the passage bunches air into less space, increasing its effective density. It also increases the restoring response when that region compresses and expands.

**The two changes do not automatically cancel**, because they act through different local features of a mode. Added mass matters where air has back-and-forth motion. Added stiffness matters where neighboring air portions repeatedly compress and expand.
At a region with **strong displacement and little compression**, added mass slows the vibration, while extra stiffness contributes little. The relevant formant **falls**.
At a region with **little displacement and strong compression**, added mass contributes little, while added stiffness strengthens the restoring action. The relevant formant **rises**.

The places with greatest movement alternate with the places with greatest compression. **One narrowing can therefore move two formants in opposite directions** when the same location is motion-dominated in one mode and compression-dominated in another.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: The highlighted tract location is **the same physical place in mode 1 and mode 2**. The two rows isolate different ways the same air can move, so they can show different local behavior at that one location.

**F1 is the frequency of mode 1, and F2 is the frequency of mode 2.** For the uniform reference, F2 is three times F1. A constriction changes the reference by making selected air elements effectively heavier and their restoring stiffness greater.

To determine the effect on either formant, the relevant distinction is **motion versus compression at the constriction**. Strong back-and-forth motion makes the added mass important; strong changes in spacing make the added stiffness important.
children: A narrowing near the /i/ location can lower F1 because mode 1 moves there, while raising F2 because mode 2 compresses there. Both effects come from the same constriction.

teaching.text: At the open lips, both modes have strong displacement, so local mass loading lowers both frequencies. Moving the narrowing toward the back changes the local pattern again, allowing F1 to rise while F2 falls.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, rounding the lips narrows the passage at the **free end**. This is **free-end loading**: the air near the lips becomes effectively heavier, while its stiffness also increases.
At the open end, the air travels back and forth strongly in **both mode 1 and mode 2**. Neighboring portions move together with little local squeezing or expansion.
children: The added effective mass therefore matters in both modes. The extra stiffness contributes little because local compression is small.

teaching.text: More moving mass makes each mode harder to turn around. Both modes slow, giving **F1 down and F2 down**. This is a prediction from the local motion of the air, rather than a separate memorized rule about the vowel.
A measured **schwa-to-/u/** transition shows the formants moving downward. The first formant can lie far below the schwa reference, consistent with the heavier moving air at the lips.
children: Exact frequencies vary across voices. The relevant comparison is the change within a voice as the lips round.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** is near **two-thirds of the distance from the closed glottal end**. The tongue narrows one region, so both local effective mass and stiffness increase there.
In **mode 1**, the air at that region mostly moves back and forth. Added mass therefore has the stronger effect, making the mode slower and **lowering F1**.
In **mode 2**, the air at the same region mostly compresses and expands. Added stiffness has the stronger effect, making the restoring action faster and **raising F2**.
The combined result is **low F1 and high F2**. The opposite directions do not require two separate constrictions; they result from one location participating differently in the two modes.
children: A measured transition from schwa into /i/ shows F1 dropping and F2 rising, matching this prediction.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** lies farther back, near **one-third of the distance from the glottis**. It affects a different part of the air’s mode patterns from the front constriction for /i/.
In **mode 1**, that back region has strong compression and expansion. More stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so the vibration speeds up and **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, the constriction falls in a region with stronger back-and-forth air displacement, between strongly compressing regions. Added moving mass slows that pattern, so **F2 falls**.
**Higher F1 and lower F2** bring the two resonances closer together. Measurements of /a/ show that same pattern, with the second formant not far above the first.
children: The result reverses /i/ because the constriction has moved, while the rules connecting moving mass, restoring stiffness and frequency stay the same.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The separate **mode 1, mode 2 and mode 3** rows isolate resonant patterns of the same air in the same tract. Their frequencies are called **F1, F2 and F3**.

Each pattern alternates between regions of **large displacement** and regions of **large compression changes**. Air elements that keep similar spacing while traveling together are showing strong mass motion. Elements that bunch together and spread apart are showing strong springiness.
The closed end remains a displacement node, and the open lip end allows strong movement. Higher modes add internal nodes and more alternating regions within that same length.
children: A point staying still throughout a mode is a node. Briefly crossing the resting position during a cycle does not make a moving point a node.

teaching.text: **The location and the mode must both be specified** when explaining a constriction’s effect. Added mass slows modes that move strongly there. Added stiffness speeds modes that compress strongly there. This is why identical physical narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: **F0 is the fundamental frequency of the vocal-fold source.** The harmonics occur at multiples of F0. In one example F0 is 100 Hz, giving harmonics at 100, 200 and 300 Hz; at F0 of 250 Hz, the first harmonics are 250, 500 and 750 Hz.
**Mass and stiffness affect F0.** Heavier, looser vocal folds have greater moving mass and less restoring stiffness, which favors a lower F0. Lighter, tighter folds favor a higher F0.
children: A higher F0 gives fewer, more widely separated harmonic lines within the same frequency range. The 350 Hz example therefore has wider spacing than the 100 Hz example.

teaching.text: F0 also changes **within a voice during speech**. Muscles alter vocal-fold stiffness, changing the repetition rate of the source. These pitch changes can contribute to how an utterance is understood.

In **“The dog slept here”** and **“The dog slept here?”**, the same words can have different F0 contours. A falling ending supports the statement pattern in the example, while a rising ending supports the question pattern.
children: The distinction concerns changes in the source frequency, rather than a change from F1 to F2. F1 and F2 are separate air resonances that shape the harmonics.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The **vocal-tract filter** is the shaped air passage above the vocal folds. Its resonances are **formants**. They depend on the tract’s shape and the local mass and stiffness of its air, rather than being the same thing as the source’s F0.

For the **schwa reference**, the first two targets are about **500 and 1,500 Hz**. The /u/ targets are lower, **/i/** has a low F1 and high F2, and **/a/** brings F1 and F2 closer together. The locations of the constrictions explain these different patterns.
children: These are **reference values**. The actual formants vary with **vocal-tract length** and the air’s mass and stiffness.

teaching.text: **A formant favors nearby harmonics.** A source harmonic close to a formant becomes strong in the output; harmonics farther away become weaker. The filter changes how much of each available source frequency is transmitted.
children: The filter does not add a new harmonic at every formant. If a formant lies between harmonic lines, the neighboring available harmonics carry the effect.

teaching.text: The narrow harmonic lines identify the source frequencies. The broad pattern of their strengths reveals the **spectral envelope**, which reflects the vowel filter. **Source spacing and filter shape describe different properties of the same sound.**

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: The grid holds **one vowel filter fixed within each column** and changes the source F0 across the rows. The formant targets mark the same resonances down a column; the harmonic frequencies become more widely spaced from the 100 Hz row to the 250 Hz and 350 Hz rows.
With **dense harmonics**, many source lines fall around each formant. Their different heights trace the broad resonant peak clearly, so the formant envelope is easier to identify.

With **sparse harmonics**, few lines fall near a formant, and a target can lie between the available frequencies. The spectrum can therefore make the resonance look weak or ambiguous even though the vowel filter has not changed.
children: Changing F0 changes where the source samples the filter. It does not by itself require the tract’s formants to move.

teaching.text: **High-pitched singing and small children’s voices** illustrate the same difficulty. Wider harmonic spacing leaves less information about the broad resonances, making some vowels harder to distinguish or their formants harder to locate.
children: Changing mouth shape can bring a resonance closer to an available harmonic. That changes the filter to improve its alignment with the source.

teaching.text: A **spectral slice in Praat** can show the harmonics at one moment. The lowest harmonic gives F0, and the spacing to the next harmonics checks that source pattern. A formant is identified from the envelope of harmonic strengths rather than by assuming the tallest individual line is itself a resonance.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** has frequency on one axis and amplitude on the other, describing a short instant. A **spectrogram** arranges many such instants across time so the changing speech sound can be followed.

In a spectrogram, **time runs horizontally**, **frequency runs vertically** and **amplitude becomes darkness**. Stronger energy is darker; weaker energy is lighter. The strong frequency regions form bands as time progresses.
For **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the first two bands are far apart. Moving toward **/a/** raises F1 and lowers F2, bringing the bands closer.
children: The band trajectories describe changing vocal-tract resonances. They are not air particles traveling up or down the frequency axis; the air itself oscillates along the tract while the measured resonant frequencies change.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **“Where were you a year ago?” changes its sound continuously.** A spectrogram of the phrase places successive moments along the time axis, frequencies vertically and stronger energy in darker regions.

During **/i/-like portions**, the example shows a high F2 together with a low F1. A constriction in the front region increases stiffness where mode 2 compresses and adds mass where mode 1 moves, explaining those separated resonances.
During the **/u/ portion in “you,”** the formants move downward. Lip rounding loads the moving free end, which lowers the relevant air resonances.
children: Across the phrase, the bands keep changing as the tongue and lips move between sounds. Reading the formant paths therefore explains a sequence of changing tract shapes rather than one steady vowel.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: A speaker produces **“ma” and “na.”** The **m portion from “ma”** is combined with the **a portion from “na.”** Although the copied consonant comes from “ma,” listeners hear the combined result as **“na.”**

The following vowel contains information about the consonant. In the example, the **a after m** has a relatively stationary formant, while the **a after n** contains a pronounced downward formant movement.
children: That change is in a **formant of the vocal-tract air**, rather than the source F0. Carrying the vowel from “na” into the splice carries the cue that supports hearing n.

teaching.text: **Speech perception combines information across time.** A listener’s consonant decision can depend strongly on the vowel that follows, so interpreting one isolated slice and assigning it a final sound label misses important information.

A speech-recognition system must therefore use relationships across a stretch of sound. The experiment demonstrates why recognizing speech requires temporal context, rather than a separate irreversible decision about every small acoustic piece.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network can use formants to decide which vowel was spoken**. Each recording supplies two input numbers: **F1**, the first air resonance, and **F2**, the second air resonance.

Different vowels produce different combinations of those two measurements. A **low F1 and high F2** supports an /i/ response such as **dean**. The input numbers describe the recording; the output identifies a vowel category.
The network’s **weights, written W**, determine how it turns the input numbers into a decision. **Learning changes the weights** using examples paired with their correct vowel labels.
children: A network that has only random starting weights can process the inputs and still give a poor answer. Performing a calculation and having learned a useful vowel decision are different achievements.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The network has **two input neurons**, one for F1 and one for F2. A neuron here is a numerical processing unit. The input units receive the measurements and pass them onward.

The three **hidden layers** have **3, 2 and 4 neurons**. They are hidden because they lie between the inputs and the final outputs. Each layer produces a new set of activations, the numbers passed to the following layer.
The network is **fully connected**: every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next. Each connection has a **weight**, which determines the contribution of its incoming value.

An **inner product** multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight and adds the results. Each processing neuron uses this operation to produce its activity. This version is **purely linear**, with no activation function inserted between the hidden layers.
The **five output neurons** correspond to **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**. The network maps one pair of formants through the hidden layers into a decision among those five vowel categories.
children: There are five layers when the input layer is counted: one input layer, three hidden layers and one output layer. The input layer receives values rather than performing the weighted processing.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: The example input is **F1 = 320 Hz and F2 = 2,000 Hz**. Its low F1 and high F2 have the /i/ pattern, so a useful network should favor **dean**.
Every connection has a **random starting weight**, a positive or negative number. These weights are the network’s adjustable knowledge, and a random initial set is not yet tuned to the vowel task.

Each neuron multiplies its incoming values by their own weights and adds the results. A **positive weight** preserves an incoming contribution’s sign; a **negative weight** reverses it. With the positive formant inputs, positive and negative weights therefore contribute in opposite directions.
children: The first processing layer combines two inputs into three activations. Those activations become the inputs used by the following layer. The weight values can change the decision because they change these contributions.

teaching.text: **Inputs describe a recording; weights describe how it is processed.** Supplying a different recording changes F1 and F2. Training changes the weights so that the same kinds of recordings lead to better vowel decisions.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In **forward propagation**, the formant input moves through the network one layer at a time. Each layer combines incoming activations with its weights and produces the activities supplied to the following layer.
The final display is a **probability distribution over five words**, written **p(word)**. Its values are 0.5 for done, 0.1 each for dune, dean and Don, and 0.2 for Dan.
children: These probabilities add to one. The largest value is assigned to done, so that is the network’s decision in the example.

teaching.text: **A valid probability distribution can still give the wrong answer.** The input’s low F1 and high F2 support dean, but the largest output probability favors done. The random weights allow processing without supplying useful vowel knowledge.

The correct answer can be represented by **0, 0, 1, 0, 0** in the output order done, dune, dean, Don and Dan. The single one identifies dean; the zeros identify the alternatives that are not the target.

**Stochastic gradient descent** changes the weights gradually using the mismatch between the predicted output and the target. The goal is for a later forward pass on this formant pattern to assign more probability to dean.
children: The formant input and the correct label supply the training example. Learning improves the network’s weights rather than changing the correct label to agree with its initial decision.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** provides tools for specifying this network in Python. **import torch** loads the library, and **import torch.nn as nn** makes its neural-network components available under the shorter name **nn**.
**nn.Sequential** arranges the processing layers in order. The output of one layer becomes the input to the next, matching the forward flow through the network.

**nn.Linear(2, 3)** receives two values and produces three. The next lines convert three to two, two to four and four to five. These numbers describe the layer widths, not the particular formant values.
children: Each output size must match the following layer’s input size. The four Linear lines specify the three hidden layers and the final output layer; the two-value input is received rather than specified as its own Linear processing line.

teaching.text: A **Linear** layer forms weighted sums, the inner products of its inputs with its weights. A **bias** is an extra added constant. **bias=False** removes that constant, and no activation functions are inserted, keeping this network purely linear.
children: A **weight matrix** has one row for each receiving neuron and one column for each incoming value. For **Linear(2, 3)**, three receiving neurons each need weights for the two inputs, so the matrix has **three rows and two columns**.

teaching.text: **Declaring a network is different from training it.** These lines specify its structure and processing order. They do not load vowel examples, compare outputs with targets or update the weights, so the declaration by itself has not learned the vowel categories.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: A **neural network** processes numerical inputs to make a decision. This vowel recognizer receives **F1 and F2**, the first two vocal-tract resonances measured in **hertz**, and chooses among the vowels in **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
children: The two input neurons receive one recording’s measurements. Three **hidden layers** process them between the input and the five output neurons, one for each vowel alternative.
The diagram’s **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** sizes count neurons in successive layers. These counts describe the network’s structure, not the activation value inside a neuron.

teaching.text: The network is **fully connected**, meaning every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has a **weight**, often written **W**, that controls its contribution to the receiving neuron.
children: The weights hold the network’s learned knowledge. Their signs and **magnitudes**, their sizes apart from the sign, determine how incoming values combine.

The weights leaving F1 and F2 are small because the formants are large values in hertz. Small weights can turn those measurements into more modest hidden-layer values. The illustrated weights stay fixed while the network produces an answer.

teaching.text: The **architecture** is the arrangement of layers and neurons. Its useful size is not known just by naming the task.
children: Different layer counts and widths can be tested by how well the network recognizes vowels. Adding processing units gives more adjustable connections; testing determines whether the change helps.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries an input through the layers to an answer. Each neuron computes an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their connection weights and adding the products.
children: The example input is **F1 = 320 Hz** and **F2 = 2,000 Hz**, a low-F1, high-F2 vowel. In **w₁F1 + w₂F2**, w₁ and w₂ name the two weights entering the top hidden neuron.
The F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Together they produce the displayed **−0.4 activation**. An activation is the neuron’s current response, shown inside its circle.
The number **−0.4 also occurs on a connection**. There it is a weight. Position distinguishes a neuron’s response from a connection’s multiplying factor.

teaching.text: This illustrated network has **no biases**, which would be extra constants added to the sums, and no hidden activation functions. Each hidden neuron passes its **linear activation**, its plain weighted sum, to the next layer.
children: One layer’s activations become the next layer’s inputs. A change in an early response therefore affects the later calculations, even while their weights remain fixed.
Making an answer using the current weights is **inference**. The essential operation here is repeated multiplication and addition, rather than a different rule for each hidden neuron.
The arithmetic is a **model of brain processing**. Real neurons use **chemical and electrical activity**; the network represents their influence through numbers, addition and multiplication.

teaching.text: The output layer first produces **scores**, also called **logits**. **Softmax** converts those scores together into a **probability distribution** over the five vowels.
children: In the displayed notation, **zᵢ** is one vowel’s raw score and **pᵢ** is its probability. The index i selects a vowel, and **Σ** means to add across the alternatives.

The probabilities run from zero to one and add up to one. A percentage expresses the same value on a zero-to-100 scale. A higher score gives a higher probability; raising one alternative’s score reduces the others’ shares.
The largest probability is **55.7% for done**, so the network chooses done. A probability describes confidence in a vowel category, not a formant frequency.

teaching.text: **Setting selected connection weights to zero** removes their contributions from the model. Comparing recognition before and after that change reveals how the removed processing affected the decision.
children: Human observations of perception after loss of particular brain functions can help determine how the network model is built. The model can then test ideas about how remaining processing might compensate.
Human evidence can improve the model, while controlled changes to the model can help investigate the roles of different processing parts.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: The top neuron in the last hidden layer has a **positive activation, 1.57**, and its connection into **done** has a **positive weight, 0.1**. Their product contributes positively to done’s output score.
children: If that activation increases while the weight stays fixed, its positive contribution becomes larger. Done’s score rises, so its probability rises.
If the weight increases while the activation stays fixed, the contribution also becomes larger. The same probability therefore rises for either of these changes.

teaching.text: The **activation** is the value passed onward, while the **weight** scales that value at the receiving neuron. The two changes affect the same positive contribution through these different roles.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: The **computed output** is the network’s prediction. The **desired output**, or **target**, records the vowel that produced the formants. Here the network favors done, but the recording is **/i/, as in dean**.
children: A **one-hot encoding** puts one in the dean position and zero in each other vowel position. It identifies the correct answer for this recording.
Random initial weights do not yet capture the vowel patterns. Training supplies the known answer so that these weights can improve.

teaching.text: The **loss** measures the mismatch between computed and desired output. The displayed **cross-entropy loss** is large when the correct vowel receives little probability.
children: Learning should increase dean’s probability and reduce the probabilities assigned to the wrong vowels. Changing the weights changes the weighted sums, which changes those probabilities.
The target stays fixed. It is the network’s knowledge, stored in its weights, that is adjusted to better match the recording’s label.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** calculates how the loss depends on the weights, starting at the output and working toward the earlier layers. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or **SGD**, uses that calculation to make gradual weight adjustments.
children: In **W ← W − η ∂L/∂W**, **W** is a weight, **L** is the loss and **η** is the learning rate, which sets the update size. The arrow means to replace W with its adjusted value.
The **gradient**, written **∂L/∂W**, says how a small increase in that weight would change the loss. The subtraction moves the weight in the direction that reduces the loss.
The forward-pass activations remain available for the backward calculation. A new forward pass uses the updated weights to calculate a new prediction.

teaching.text: The useful direction can differ from connection to connection. A weight from a **positive activation into dean** can increase to support the correct answer, while a positive contribution into **done** should decrease.
children: With a **negative incoming activation**, decreasing the weight into dean increases that input’s contribution to dean’s score. Supporting the correct answer therefore does not require every weight to increase.
The illustrated input-layer weights change only slightly. Their scale and updates reflect the large formant values in hertz, rather than requiring every layer’s weights to move by an equal amount.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the **circled final weight, +0.1**, the incoming activation is **+1.57** and the destination is **done**. Increasing that weight increases done’s score and probability.
children: Dean is the target, so making done more likely increases the error. Decreasing this marked weight reduces its positive contribution to the wrong answer.
This is a conclusion about this connection’s signs and destination, not a rule that all weights should decrease.

teaching.text: The **circled early weight, +0.005 from F1**, has a less direct effect. Changing it alters a first-layer activation, which alters later activations before the output probabilities change.
children: Along that route, the change combines with many other positive and negative weights. Its final effect cannot be determined from the early connection alone.

The backward calculation accounts for those intervening operations to determine which change reduces the final error. A small coefficient is not automatically an easy or unimportant influence to assess.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **W5** labels the last set of processing weights and **W2** the first set. These are names for groups of connections at different positions in the network, not individual weights equal to five or two.

The last weights have the **most direct influence on the output error**. Their effect reaches the probabilities without passing through more hidden layers, so that part of the problem is easier to calculate.
children: An early weight changes its own layer’s activation, then later layers’ activations, before reaching the probabilities. Its contribution to the error therefore **includes the effects of the later weights**.

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming** solves dependent problems by solving the simpler parts and reusing their results in the larger calculation. Working backward makes the output-side error information available when earlier weights are considered.
children: This is the Bellman–Viterbi principle applied to the learning calculation. The difficult early-weight problem contains the downstream parts already calculated near the output.

The combined procedure uses **SGD for gradual weight changes** and **dynamic programming for the backward organization and reuse of calculations**. Ordinary prediction still carries the input forward.

teaching.text: The forward–backward arrangement also motivates comparisons with **biological neurons**. The numerical model makes the forward response and the backward learning influence explicit, so their relationship to nervous-system processing can be investigated.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training requires an **input matrix** and a matching **target matrix**. A matrix is a table of numbers, with one row for each recording in this example.
children: **Formant_Inputs, 110 × 2** has 110 rows and the two measurement columns **F1 and F2**. **TrueVowel_Outputs, 110 × 5** has the corresponding rows and five vowel-answer columns.
Only a few illustrative rows are visible. The printed 110 describes the full row count of these example tables, rather than the number of formants in one recording.

teaching.text: Each target row is a **one-hot answer**, with one for the true vowel and zeros for the others in the order **done, dune, dean, Don, Dan**.
children: The highlighted **320 and 2,000 Hz** measurements have their one in the **dean** column. The five target entries describe one recording’s answer, rather than five separate recordings.

teaching.text: The rows must **stay aligned across the two tables**. A row of formants from done must be paired with the target for done, and the same pairing must hold for every row.
children: Reordering only one table would train the network using incorrect answers. During learning, the target remains fixed while the weights change to bring the computed output closer to it.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: The **import** commands make the **PyTorch** library available. A library supplies reusable code, so the program can request neural-network operations without writing their internal calculations.
children: **import torch** provides PyTorch, and **from torch import nn** supplies its neural-network tools under the name **nn**.

**torch.load** reads the saved formant and target tables into **X** and **Y**. **float** puts their entries in a number format that supports decimal values. The shown shapes are **110 × 2** inputs and **110 × 5** targets.

teaching.text: The variable **net** holds the network. **nn.Sequential** runs its processing layers in the stated order, and **nn.Linear** calculates weighted sums.
children: **Linear(2, 3)** receives two values and produces three; the following processing sizes are **3 → 2**, **2 → 4** and **4 → 5**. Each layer’s output count fits the next layer’s input count.
There are **five layers in the diagram but four Linear instructions**. The input layer only receives F1 and F2; it does not perform a separate weighted-sum calculation.

teaching.text: The learning commands compare the network’s answers with the targets and adjust its weights.
children: **net(X)** processes the input table. **CrossEntropyLoss** compares those computed scores with **Y**, handling the probability-related loss calculation. The variable **loss** stores that mismatch.
**SGD** specifies stochastic gradient descent. **net.parameters()** supplies the trainable parameters, and **lr = 0.1** sets the learning rate, or step size.
**zero_grad()** clears old stored gradient information. **loss.backward()** calculates how the loss depends on the weights, and **sgd.step()** applies the weight update.

teaching.text: This is **one training step using all 110 rows together**, not an entire repeated training run. The code’s default initialization gives it its own starting parameters, so its numerical outputs do not reproduce the hand-picked weights in the illustration.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: An **activation function** changes a neuron’s weighted sum into the response it passes on. The **sigmoid**, written **σ**, is an S-shaped function that maps the weighted sum **z** into a value between zero and one.
children: The graph’s horizontal **Linear Activation** axis is z, the inner product. The vertical **Sigmoid Activation** axis is **σ(z)**, the resulting response.
The marked pairs **(−4, 0.018)** and **(4, 0.982)** show input followed by output. A strongly negative sum gives a response near zero, and a strongly positive sum gives one near one.

teaching.text: The sigmoid’s **steep middle and flat ends** make its sensitivity depend on the input.
children: Near the middle, an input change produces a relatively strong change in response. At either flat end, even quite different inputs can produce nearly the same response.

In **animal perception**, similar inputs can be perceived differently, while larger input differences can sometimes be perceived as the same. The curve illustrates how processing can emphasize some differences and reduce others.

teaching.text: The biological motivation associated with **Adrian’s** work concerns neurons’ **near-digital behavior**, meaning responses close to **on or off**. Artificial neurons combine many incoming influences through their weighted sums; sigmoid adds a bounded response rather than allowing any sum to pass on unchanged.
children: The model still allows intermediate activations. A value between zero and one is one neuron’s response, not automatically a probability distribution over the five vowels.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The demonstration changes hidden neurons from **linear** responses to **sigmoid** responses one at a time, while keeping **the input and every weight fixed**.
children: The inputs stay **F1 = 320 Hz** and **F2 = 2,000 Hz**. **Purple** marks hidden neurons still passing their linear sums; **green** marks neurons with sigmoid applied.
The three hidden layers contain **3, 2 and 4 neurons**, so nine hidden neurons switch in layer order.

teaching.text: For the first switch, a weighted sum just below zero becomes a sigmoid response just below one half. The neuron therefore sends a **positive value where its linear activation was negative**.
children: That new value changes the inputs to later neurons. **Every downstream sum and activation must be recalculated** using the updated layer before it, rather than applying sigmoid to a list of old linear results.
The label **Hidden layer 3, neuron 4** locates a particular unit. In **σ(−0.076) = 0.481**, −0.076 is its current weighted sum and 0.481 the value passed on after sigmoid.

teaching.text: The network’s preferred vowel changes as the processing rule changes. Done begins with the largest probability; its lead shrinks, Don briefly leads, and Dan eventually has the largest probability.
children: With every hidden neuron using sigmoid, **Dan has 32%** and **dean has 23%**. These are final output probabilities, produced by **softmax**, and all five still sum to one.

The answer has changed, but dean is still not the top answer. **This is not learning**: no weight was adjusted using a target. Changing the activation rule affects behavior without automatically correcting the decision.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program adds **nn.Sigmoid()** after each hidden **nn.Linear** layer. Linear calculates the weighted sum, and Sigmoid changes that result before it enters the next layer.
children: Sigmoid follows **Linear(2, 3)**, **Linear(3, 2)** and **Linear(2, 4)**. It changes each value separately but keeps the same count, so the layer sizes remain **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.
**X** contains the input formants, **Y** the correct-vowel targets, and **net** the network that processes X.

teaching.text: The last **Linear(4, 5)** supplies five final scores to **CrossEntropyLoss** without a hidden sigmoid after it.
children: **Sigmoid** bounds each hidden neuron separately. **Softmax** treats the final scores together to form probabilities that add up to one; the loss handles the related probability calculation when comparing scores with targets.
The training procedure still uses **SGD**, the learning rate, **backward** and **step**. Default starting parameters mean the program does not reproduce the illustration’s exact numerical outputs.

teaching.text: **ReLU** is another activation function that can replace sigmoid in a network. Comparing recognition performance after such a change tests whether that processing rule helps or hurts this vowel task.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** recognizes an isolated vowel from **F1 and F2**, the first two vocal-tract resonances in **hertz**. Its five possible answers are **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
children: The two input neurons receive one recording’s formants. Three hidden layers process those numbers, and five output neurons represent the competing vowel answers.
The **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** widths count neurons. An **activation** is the numerical response produced by a particular neuron, not the number of neurons in its layer.

teaching.text: Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, making the network **fully connected**. The numbers on those connections are **weights**, its learned knowledge.
children: Each weight scales an incoming value before the receiving neuron adds the contributions. With positive inputs, positive weights add and negative weights subtract; the **magnitude**, or size apart from the sign, controls the strength of that contribution.
The illustrated weights stay fixed during a prediction. Learning changes them, while a new recording supplies new formant inputs.

teaching.text: Training starts from **random weights**, so the network’s initial answer can be wrong. A **one-hot target** identifies the true vowel with one in its position and zeros in the others.
children: For a dean recording, only the dean target entry is one. Comparing that desired output with the computed output supplies the error used to improve the weights.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** processes the input layer by layer through **inner products**. Each receiving neuron multiplies incoming values by their weights and adds the products.
children: The example supplies **320 Hz for F1** and **2,000 Hz for F2**. In **w₁F1 + w₂F2**, the two weights control how these measurements contribute to the top hidden neuron.

Its F1 contribution is positive and its F2 contribution is negative, producing the displayed **−0.4 activation**. Increasing F1 with the weights fixed raises this neuron’s sum; increasing F2 lowers it.
A number inside a hidden circle is an **activation**, while a number on a connection is a **weight**. The repeated −0.4 occurs in both roles, so its location matters.

teaching.text: A layer’s activation values become the next layer’s inputs. The same kind of weighted-sum processing continues through the hidden layers until the output has one score for each vowel.
children: For this **linear** illustration, the hidden neurons pass on their sums without an extra activation function.

teaching.text: **Softmax** turns the final **scores, or logits zᵢ**, into **probabilities pᵢ**. The index i identifies a vowel, and **Σ** in the expression adds across the alternatives.
children: The probabilities total one. A larger score gives a larger probability, and increasing one score reduces the probability shares of the other vowels.

Done receives the largest probability, about **55.7%**, so the network selects done. The input is /i/, as in dean, so this decision differs from the known answer. The confidence values describe vowel alternatives, not frequencies in hertz.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: The diagram’s positive **1.57 hidden activation** feeds done through a positive **0.1 weight**. Increasing either one, while holding the other fixed, increases their positive contribution to done’s score.
children: A higher done score gives a higher done probability. The activation is the value sent onward; the weight is the multiplier on that connection.

teaching.text: The **activation** is the value passed onward, and the **weight** scales its contribution to the receiving neuron. The output changes because either adjustment makes this positive contribution larger.

sections.title: Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The scatterplot shows **525 recordings**, with **105 tokens**, or recorded examples, of each vowel. **F1 runs horizontally** and **F2 vertically**, both in **Hz**.
children: Every point is one recording. Moving right means higher F1; moving up means higher F2. The legend uses red for dean, magenta for Dan, blue for dune, cyan for Don and green for schwa in done.

teaching.text: Each vowel forms a **cloud of points** because speakers and recordings vary. Dean generally has **low F1 and high F2**, while Dan extends toward higher F1.
children: Dune, Don and done have much more **overlap**. A new pair of formants in that shared region can be compatible with several vowel categories.
Some unusual points can be measurement errors, but the recorded data are retained. Real recognition must deal with imperfect observations as well as ordinary differences between speakers.

teaching.text: Overlap limits what these **two input measurements** can identify. If two recordings have identical F1 and F2 but different vowel labels, the network receives the same input for both. It cannot tell them apart from those two numbers alone.
children: The network has to learn useful patterns across the data instead of finding a single isolated position for each vowel. Repeated exposure improves the learned decision, but does not create information absent from F1 and F2.

teaching.text: **Peterson and Barney** also found substantial overlap when measuring vowels across speakers. **Normalization** attempts to reduce differences between speakers, such as differences associated with vocal-tract length, but it does not make this recognition problem automatically simple.
children: A static pair of formants omits the way speech changes over time. Models that process sequences can use broader temporal context, including information around a sound, rather than having to decide from that pair alone.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: The **Computed Output** gives the network’s current probabilities. The **Desired Output** is the known vowel in **one-hot form**: one for dean and zeros for done, dune, Don and Dan.
children: The illustrated network puts most probability on done and little on dean. Its **loss**, the mismatch with the target, is therefore substantial. Increasing dean’s probability lowers the cross-entropy loss.

teaching.text: The learning procedure combines **backpropagation**, **SGD** and **dynamic programming**. The backward calculation determines how the loss depends on the weights; SGD uses that information to make gradual updates.
children: Calculation starts near the outputs and proceeds toward the input, reusing the saved forward activations. An earlier weight’s influence includes the intervening layers, so the later-layer effects are needed to calculate it.

In **W ← W − η ∂L/∂W**, W is a weight, L the loss and η the learning rate. The **gradient ∂L/∂W** tells how raising W would affect L; subtracting that gradient directs the adjustment toward lower loss.

teaching.text: The useful weight change depends on the incoming activation and the destination.
children: A weight carrying a **positive activation into dean** can increase to strengthen the correct answer. With a **negative incoming activation**, decreasing its weight instead increases that input’s contribution to dean’s score.
A positive contribution into **done**, the wrong answer, should decrease. These different directions are consistent with the same goal of reducing the error.

The small weights leaving the large formant values change only slightly in the illustration. An update’s size depends on the role and scale of the connection, rather than being identical at every layer.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The **circled +0.1 connection** carries the positive **1.57 activation** into done. Raising that weight raises done’s score and probability, directly increasing support for the wrong answer.
children: Because dean is the target, the useful direction for this connection is **down**. A smaller positive weight contributes less to done.

teaching.text: The **circled +0.005 connection from F1** acts much earlier. A change there alters first-layer activations, which alter the second and third layers before changing the probabilities.
children: The later weights can combine that change in different directions. Its useful adjustment cannot be inferred from the early weight’s sign or size alone.

This is why a purely **greedy choice**, based only on an immediate local effect, can miss the consequence for the final answer. Backpropagation accounts for the dependent calculations through the network.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **W2** names the first set of processing weights and **W5** the last. The last weights have the **most direct effect on the output error**, while early weights act through the layers between them and the output.

The early-weight problem **contains the downstream calculations**. To find how an early connection affects the loss, the calculation needs to know how the changes it produces are transformed by the later layers.
children: **Dynamic programming** solves and reuses those simpler dependent parts. Calculating the output-side error first makes its information available when an earlier layer is considered.
The backward order avoids repeatedly solving the same downstream problem for every early connection.

teaching.text: In the combined learning procedure, **SGD** adjusts weights gradually and **dynamic programming** organizes the backward calculation. The Bellman–Viterbi principle explains the reuse of dependent results, rather than treating each connection’s influence as an unrelated problem.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: The two **training matrices** pair recordings with known answers. **Formant_Inputs, 110 × 2** has recording rows and the **F1/F2** columns; **TrueVowel_Outputs, 110 × 5** has matching rows and five vowel columns.
children: The printed 110 is this example table’s row count. Only a few illustrative rows are visible. A target’s single one identifies the true vowel, and its four zeros exclude the other alternatives.
For the highlighted **320 and 2,000 Hz** input, the one is in **dean**. Each input row must remain aligned with its own target row.

teaching.text: A matched row pair supplies one **labeled training example**. The network processes the formants with its current weights, compares its computed output with the fixed target and uses the mismatch to improve the weights.
children: Choosing the correct vowel does not automatically mean the whole probability distribution matches its one-hot target. A confident correct output has little loss, while a less confident correct choice can still leave loss to reduce.
Getting some examples right therefore does not establish that the network has learned the general pattern. It can fit familiar examples without capturing a useful generalization.

teaching.text: The language-learning example concerns **memorization, generalization and exceptions**. In Carol Chomsky’s example, children first produce **go/went** correctly, then apply the regular past-tense **-ed** pattern, as in **jump/jumped**, to produce **goed**. They later learn the irregular exception.
children: The intermediate error can reflect learning a real pattern, rather than simply forgetting a correct answer. Correct familiar forms at one stage do not by themselves demonstrate complete knowledge of the rule and its exceptions.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: The **PyTorch import** commands provide reusable tools for neural-network processing and learning. **torch.load** reads the input formants into **X** and the target answers into **Y**; **float** puts the entries in a decimal-capable number format.
children: The code’s **110 × 2** and **110 × 5** comments count recording rows and measurement or target columns in these example tables.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** places the processing layers in order, and each **nn.Linear** takes weighted sums of incoming values.
children: The sizes **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** carry the two formants through three hidden layers to five vowel scores. Each output width matches the input width of the next layer.

The diagram has five layers but only four Linear instructions because the two input neurons receive information without a separate processing calculation. The variable **net** names this network, and **net(X)** processes X through it.

teaching.text: The learning commands use the mismatch with **Y** to adjust the weights.
children: **SGD** specifies the update method, and **net.parameters()** supplies its trainable parameters. **lr = 0.1** is the learning rate: larger steps can move learning faster but make fine adjustment less precise, while smaller steps move more gradually.
**zero_grad()** clears the previous stored gradients. **CrossEntropyLoss** compares the computed scores with Y, and **loss** stores the error measure.
**loss.backward()** calculates how that loss depends on the weights. **sgd.step()** applies the adjustment; the weights do not change merely because a prediction or a loss has been calculated.

teaching.text: This program makes **one update using all rows together**. Its default starting parameters differ from the hand-selected weights in the accompanying diagram, so the code expresses the same processing structure without promising the same intermediate numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid**, written **σ**, is an S-shaped **activation function**. It transforms a neuron’s weighted sum **z**, its linear activation, into a response between zero and one.
children: The horizontal axis plots **Linear Activation**, and the vertical axis **Sigmoid Activation**. In **σ(z)**, z is the incoming sum and σ(z) the value passed on.
The marked points show **−4 → 0.018** and **4 → 0.982**. Strongly negative sums produce responses near zero; strongly positive sums produce responses near one.

teaching.text: The steep middle and flat ends produce different kinds of sensitivity.
children: Near the middle, an input change gives a relatively strong change in response. Near either end, even quite different inputs can give almost the same response.

In **animal perception**, similar inputs can be perceived differently, while quite different inputs can be perceived as alike. The S-shape illustrates how a processing rule can emphasize or reduce differences.

teaching.text: The biological motivation associated with **Adrian’s** work concerns neurons’ **near-digital behavior**, meaning responses close to **on or off**. Sigmoid adds a bounded response to the artificial neuron’s integration of many inputs.
children: The function still permits intermediate values. Its output is an individual neuron’s activation, separate from softmax probabilities over the five vowel categories.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Applying **sigmoid** changes hidden neurons’ processing while keeping **F1 = 320 Hz, F2 = 2,000 Hz and every weight fixed**.
children: **Purple** neurons still pass their plain linear sums. **Green** neurons have sigmoid applied after their weighted sums. The three hidden layers contain three, two and four neurons, which switch one at a time in that order.

teaching.text: A changed activation becomes a changed input to the later layers. **All downstream weighted sums and activations must be recalculated** after each switch.
children: The first neuron’s slightly negative sum becomes a response just below one half, changing the sign of what it sends onward. Later responses must use that new value, rather than the old all-linear activations.

**Hidden layer 3, neuron 4** identifies a location. **σ(−0.076) = 0.481** identifies the weighted sum at that neuron and its transformed response; these decimals have a different role from the layer and neuron counts.

teaching.text: The network’s answer changes: done’s lead shrinks, Don briefly becomes most likely, and Dan eventually leads. With all hidden neurons on sigmoid, **Dan has 32% and dean 23%**.
children: The final percentages still come from **softmax** and sum to one. They describe alternative vowel probabilities, not the individual hidden activations.

Dean is still not the preferred answer. **Changing an activation function is not learning by itself**, because the weights were not adjusted from a target, even though the behavior changed substantially.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program inserts **nn.Sigmoid()** after each of the three hidden **nn.Linear** layers. Linear calculates weighted sums; Sigmoid transforms the resulting values before the next layer receives them.
children: **Linear(2, 3)** produces three values, and applying sigmoid still leaves three values. The same applies to the other hidden layers, so the complete widths stay **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.
**X** contains formant inputs, **Y** contains correct vowel targets, and **net(X)** processes the inputs through the network.

teaching.text: The final **Linear(4, 5)** produces five scores without a hidden sigmoid after it. **CrossEntropyLoss** compares those scores with the targets and handles the softmax-related loss calculation.
children: Sigmoid acts on hidden neurons separately. The final probability calculation treats the five vowel alternatives together, so the two operations have different jobs.

teaching.text: The learning instructions still clear gradients, compute the loss, run **backward** and apply **SGD step** using the learning rate. The default starting parameters do not reproduce the illustrative diagram’s hand-picked intermediate values.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: **Initialization** is the choice of starting weights. **Seed 0** identifies the random starting point for this run of the linear vowel network.
children: The model has the **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** processing widths, with **bias=False** and no hidden activation functions. Its trainable weights are repeatedly adjusted using the same vowel data.
In the code, **X = Formant_Inputs / 1000** expresses the inputs in **kilohertz instead of hertz**. The recordings and their relative formant relationships stay the same.

teaching.text: The graph plots **training accuracy**, the percentage of training recordings whose highest output score selects the correct vowel. The horizontal **Epoch** axis counts training passes, and the vertical axis gives percent correct.
children: Here a pass uses all **525 training recordings** for a full-batch update, repeated **2,000 times** at learning rate **0.1**. The plotted accuracy is measured on these same recordings, rather than on a separate set of new examples.
With **five possible vowels**, random guessing is correct one time in five. This **chance level is 20%**. An untrained network can therefore get some answers right without useful vowel knowledge.

teaching.text: The curve begins near chance, then rises clearly above it. It briefly dips toward chance, recovers and levels off at **44.95%**, a little below half.
children: A flat period is a **plateau**: further updates make little visible difference to accuracy. The improvement above chance shows useful learning, while the plateau shows that the decisions remain far from perfect.
The loop can still adjust weights during a flat accuracy period. Accuracy counts the winning category, so unchanged category choices can leave the percentage flat despite numerical updates.

teaching.text: The program’s variables separate training from measuring the result.
children: **model** is the network, **loss_fn** measures cross-entropy error and **opt** applies SGD updates. **y** holds the correct category selected from each one-hot target by **argmax**, which finds the largest entry.
Each pass clears old gradients, computes the loss, runs **backward** and calls **step**. The **no_grad** section measures the result without calculating another learning update.

**pred** selects each recording’s largest output score, **correct** is the fraction matching y, and **accuracy** saves the percentages for plotting. The **plt** commands display those saved values against Epoch.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: The training is repeated for **ten initializations**, keeping the data, network structure, learning rate and update count the same. Only the **starting weights** change.
children: The legend’s **Seed 0–Seed 9** labels identify those random initializations. Each run starts with a fresh model and optimizer; the seeds are not vowel categories or additional recording measurements.

teaching.text: The horizontal **Epoch** axis counts full-data training passes, and the vertical axis gives **training accuracy in percent** on the same 525 recordings.
children: The curves begin near **20% chance**. Some leave that level quickly, others remain near it longer, and several temporarily drop back. Their routes through learning differ.
All ten displayed runs finish at **44.95%**. Their curves overlap after converging, so several runs can occupy the same visible line.

teaching.text: The common plateau remains well below perfect accuracy. The formant clouds **overlap**, especially for dune, Don and done, so F1 and F2 often do not uniquely identify the vowel.
children: Changing the starting point does not supply extra information about a recording. The repeated runs take different paths and improve at different speeds, yet reach a similar final limit under the same training conditions.

teaching.text: A different **architecture or activation function** changes what processing is available. Layer counts, neuron counts and functions such as sigmoid can be varied and their measured recognition compared.
children: This is a different experiment from changing only the starting weights. A changed design is evaluated by the decisions it produces, rather than assumed to be better merely because it contains more parts.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes an input **vector**, a list of numbers, and uses its **weights** to compute a decision. The vowel example supplies **F1 and F2**, the first two formant frequencies, and chooses among **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**.
children: The two input units supply the measurements. The hidden layers have **three, two, and four units**, and the five output units represent the five vowel alternatives.
Numbers on the connections are **weights**. Their positive or negative signs determine how incoming activations contribute; they are not output probabilities.

teaching.text: **McCulloch and Pitts** proposed that simple mathematics could model aspects of nervous activity. Their **all-or-none** description distinguishes a neuron being active from being inactive.
children: The **sigmoid** is an activation function connected with this idea. It changes a weighted result toward a low or high activation, rather than leaving the weighted sum as the whole response.
The historical dates **1943–1986** mark the development of these ideas, from the early artificial-neuron proposal to more developed neural-network models.

teaching.text: **Parallel Distributed Processing** describes two important features of these networks. **Parallel** means that many neurons in one layer compute their activations at the same time.
children: **Distributed** means that information about F1 and F2 is spread across the activations of several neurons, rather than being held by one special neuron.
The activations in one layer become inputs to another. **Forward propagation** computes the response, while **backpropagation** supplies error information used to learn better weights.

teaching.text: A **static vector** is one fixed list representing one moment. A network making one decision from that list does not by itself account for how speech and language unfold through time.
children: During speech, formants change from moment to moment as the articulators move. A sentence also contains a sequence of words whose relationships extend beyond one isolated word.

The information needed for a decision can therefore include a developing sequence, rather than only a single snapshot. Modeling that sequence requires keeping the relationships between successive moments available.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: **Michael Jordan’s recurrent neural network** was developed to model **speech production**, the changing movements of articulators such as the tongue, velum, and lips.
children: **Nasality** concerns the velum’s position, and **rounding** concerns the lips. Producing a sequence requires coordinating these properties across time, rather than selecting a category from one fixed measurement.

teaching.text: The **plan units** supply information about the sequence to produce. The **hidden units** combine plan information with the current state, and the **output units** produce a response.
